questions.q: A bronchus is identified in a lung section. Which histological feature distinguishes an intrapulmonary bronchus from a bronchiole?
options: A simple squamous epithelial lining throughout
questions.explain: Intrapulmonary bronchi contain irregular cartilage plates and submucosal glands; bronchioles lack cartilage and submucosal glands.

questions.q: A small airway has no cartilage or submucosal glands and is lined mainly by ciliated cuboidal cells with club cells. What is it?
questions.explain: Bronchioles are small conducting airways without cartilage or submucosal glands; their epithelium becomes lower and includes club cells.

questions.q: Which cell type produces pulmonary surfactant and can proliferate to replace damaged alveolar epithelial cells?
questions.explain: Type II pneumocytes secrete surfactant and serve as progenitor cells capable of differentiating into type I and type II alveolar cells.

questions.q: Which alveolar cell forms most of the extremely thin surface across which oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse?
questions.explain: Type I pneumocytes are thin squamous cells covering most of the alveolar surface and forming the epithelial component of the blood–air barrier.

questions.q: A lung section shows a dust-laden phagocytic cell within an alveolar space. Which cell is this?
questions.explain: Alveolar macrophages migrate over the alveolar surface and phagocytose inhaled particles and microorganisms; they are also called dust cells.
